reasons: Same sign: our conditional yield change is negative for all four matched countries (literature route China -1.0, India -4.2, Russia -7.3, USA -6.2 %; empirical route also negative) and F4 rises in each. Like Zhao, both exclude CO2 and adaptation. China is the least affected in both. Our India wheat F4 rise is heat-driven, which matches Zhao's temperature-only framing. For Russia and China, however, our F4 rise is mainly water deficit, a pathway Zhao does not include.
cannot_establish: Cannot validate magnitudes (Zhao's %/C of global warming vs our %-change under one 2041-2060 scenario) or the country ranking (Zhao ranks India above Russia; ours ranks Russia above USA above India). Zhao is also our crop-ranking validation source, so it is not fully independent of our earlier checks.

reasons: Agrees for South Asia: Jagermeyr shows spring-wheat losses there with good model agreement, and our India wheat change is negative and heat-driven. Disagrees for China and the USA: the paper projects gains for the North China Plain and northern US winter wheat, while ours are negative. Likely reasons: the paper's wheat gains are explicitly linked to CO2 (we exclude it), the paper looks at end-century high-latitude warming, and our USA/China F4 rise is partly water-driven. The paper also reports MRI-ESM2 as the GCM with the least pessimistic impacts, so our single-GCM choice is probably mild.
cannot_establish: Cannot separate CO2 from climate in the paper's regional maps; end-century SSP5-8.5 is not 2041-2060 SSP2-4.5; the paper's regional statements are not panel-country numbers.

reasons: Our wheat losses in all six countries match Deryng's no-CO2 result, where spring wheat follows maize's negative trend, and the heat-at-flowering mechanism is shared. They do not match Deryng's headline with CO2, where spring wheat gains through the 2050s.
cannot_establish: Agreement is partly built in: our wheat T_crit/T_lim (heat damage function) are taken from Deryng Table A.1, so this is not an independent check. Deryng is spring wheat only, global, and includes planting-date/cultivar adaptation.

reasons: Both show warming lowers wheat yield (Asseng about -6 % per C of further warming; our conditional change negative in all six panel countries).
cannot_establish: Abstract only; a sensitivity per C, not a scenario; no country results to match; no water pathway.

reasons: Same direction and mechanism for India: wheat losses by 2050, larger in warmer regions, although that study includes CO2 fertilisation. Our India wheat change is negative (literature -4.2 %, empirical -6.5 %) and the F4 rise is almost entirely heat.
cannot_establish: Abstract only; SRES-era MIROC3.2.HI/PRECIS scenarios; the late-sowing effect and the sub-national pattern (central/south-central) cannot be checked with our national aggregation.

reasons: Both find a wheat yield decline in India from warming that shortens crop duration (Chandran -7 to -9 %; ours negative, heat-driven).
cannot_establish: One irrigated site in West Bengal; mid- and end-century pooled; CO2 treatment of the quoted range not stated; cannot test magnitude.

reasons: China and Bangladesh agree: Zhao finds small averaged impacts and our rice change is about 0. India does not agree on the main route: Zhao finds large losses (-6.6 % per C) while our literature-accounting route gives ~0 (+0.1 %), because monthly flowering T_eff rarely exceeds the 35 C rice threshold and India's water deficit falls. Our empirical cross-check route (-11.9 % for India) agrees with Zhao.
cannot_establish: Cannot tell whether the discrepancy is a real difference or the known monthly-resolution artefact for rice heat (daily spikelet sterility is invisible to us); per-C vs scenario metrics differ.

reasons: Neither study finds a large mid-latitude/South Asian rice loss: the paper shows rice gains in South Asia, NE China and South America, and our rice changes are near zero in India, Bangladesh, China and Brazil. The paper attributes its gains largely to CO2 (median rice CO2 effect 37 %), which we exclude, so the agreement is in sign of 'no strong loss', not in mechanism.
cannot_establish: Cannot isolate the climate-only rice response from the paper's figures; end-century; the paper finds no decisive global sign.

reasons: Rainfed rice: Soora projects only a marginal 2050 loss and gains in low-rainfall regions with more rain, which matches our near-zero India rice change and falling, water-driven F4. Irrigated rice: Soora projects a ~7 % loss by 2050; we cannot reproduce it because irrigated area carries no water stress in our index and monthly heat stays below the rice threshold.
cannot_establish: Abstract only; CO2 handling not stated in abstract; SRES scenarios; we have no irrigated-rice heat pathway at monthly resolution.

reasons: Without CO2, Chandran's rice change spans zero at mid-century RCP4.5 (-20 to +20 % across GCMs), which is compatible with our near-zero India rice result. With CO2 the paper projects gains (+11 to +40 %), which our no-CO2 index cannot show.
cannot_establish: One irrigated site; our national monthly aggregate cannot be compared with site-level GCM spread; magnitudes not comparable.

reasons: USA and Brazil match: Zhao loses and our literature-route change is negative (USA -6.6, Brazil -2.7 %). China and India do not match on the literature route (+2.1 and +0.95 %), because our maize F4 is water-dominated and the future is wetter there, whereas Zhao is temperature-only. Our empirical route is negative in all four countries, consistent with Zhao.
cannot_establish: Zhao has no water pathway and is per C of global warming; cannot attribute the China/India difference to rainfall alone without a temperature-only run.

reasons: USA matches: Jagermeyr shows losses across North America and our USA maize change is negative. China does not match on our literature route (+2.1 % vs losses with high model agreement), but our empirical route (-8.3 %) agrees. The paper's statement that MRI-ESM2 gives the least pessimistic impacts implies our single-GCM result is likely at the mild end.
cannot_establish: End-century SSP5-8.5 vs 2041-2060 SSP2-4.5; ensemble of 12 crop models x 5 GCMs vs our one GCM; cannot test the time-of-emergence result.

reasons: USA and Brazil maize losses match, as does heat at flowering as a mechanism. For China, Deryng's small CO2 gain is cancelled by heat stress (net about zero), while our literature route shows a small gain from a wetter future.
cannot_establish: Not independent: our maize T_crit/T_lim come from Deryng Table A.1. Deryng country results are 2080s RCP8.5 with CO2 and adaptation.

reasons: Closest method to ours: delta-change on observed climate, no CO2, no adaptation. The empirical route matches fully: Tigchelaar's maize losses in the USA, China, Brazil, Ukraine and India mirror our negative empirical change in all five. The literature route matches for the USA, Brazil and Ukraine (losses, F4 rises) but not China and India (small gains), where our wetter-future water term dominates; Tigchelaar holds precipitation constant. India having the smallest loss probability matches our India having the smallest dT_eff (+0.7 C).
cannot_establish: Tigchelaar is temperature-only and uses global-warming levels (+2 C ~ 2042-2055 under RCP8.5), so the rainfall part of our result cannot be checked; daily-degree-day effects are beyond our monthly data.

reasons: Brazil (tropical loss) and China (small gain) match our signs. India (marginal areas become unsuitable) and North America (+10 % suitability) do not: our India maize literature change is slightly positive and our USA change is negative.
cannot_establish: Suitability area is not yield; SRES A2, two GCMs; the Brazil -64 % is for 2100. Cannot compare magnitudes.

reasons: Brazil maize: Zilli's production losses (-12.9 to -29.4 %) match the sign of our conditional yield change (-2.7 % literature, -18.3 % empirical), and our F4 rises, mostly from water deficit. Zilli explains the loss through lower tropical productivity.
cannot_establish: Zilli's figure includes area reallocation and CO2 fertilisation, so yield and production cannot be separated; cannot confirm the mechanism (water vs heat) from GLOBIOM outputs.

reasons: Zhao's soybean signal is weak (global CIs include zero) with the largest loss in the USA; ours is likewise small and mixed (USA -4.2 %, Brazil and Argentina about -0.2 to -0.5 %, China +2.9 % on the literature route). China shows no significant effect in Zhao and a small gain in ours. Our empirical route is negative in all four countries.
cannot_establish: Only three soybean studies in Zhao; per-C metric; cannot test magnitudes.

reasons: Geographic pattern matches: losses in the USA (ours -4.2 %, F4 rises from water) and gains in parts of China and higher latitudes (ours China +2.9 %, Russia +2.7 %). For Brazil the paper shows losses while ours is near zero (-0.2 %).
cannot_establish: The paper's soybean result includes a large CO2 effect (median 48 % by 2099) and is end-century; cannot isolate the climate-only regional pattern.

reasons: USA loss and China gain match ours. India (most affected in Deryng) does not match: our India soybean change is about zero to slightly positive, with a wetter future. Argentina (large gain in Deryng) is near zero in ours.
cannot_establish: Not independent: our soybean T_crit/T_lim come from Deryng Table A.1. Country results are 2080s RCP8.5 with CO2 and adaptation.

reasons: Both find deterioration for Brazilian soybean in direction: Zilli projects production losses, and our F4 rises slightly from water while the empirical route is negative (-9.2 %). Our main literature route, however, is near zero (-0.2 %).
cannot_establish: Production with area change and CO2 vs our yield-only no-CO2 change; sub-national Matopiba concentration cannot be checked at national aggregation.

reasons: Walikar reports small soybean declines by 2050 in Madhya Pradesh (Table 3 about -5.6 to +0.5 %, from warming shortening crop duration), while our India soybean change is about zero to slightly positive (literature +0.6 %, empirical +1.6 %) and F4 falls because the future is wetter. Both magnitudes are small.
cannot_establish: GCM and CO2 treatment not reported in the paper; five districts of one state vs our national rainfed aggregate; our monthly heat threshold for soybean (35 C) is not reached, so we cannot represent duration-shortening effects.

reasons: Neither study shows a uniform large loss for Indian chickpea from climate alone. Singh: CO2-inclusive changes of +17 % (north/central) and -16 % (south), with climate-only effects site-dependent. Ours: literature route near zero (-0.2 %), empirical route negative (-9.1 %).
cannot_establish: Abstract only, so the climate-only (no-CO2) site numbers are not available; GCM/scenario not stated; cannot check the north-south contrast at national scale.

reasons: Ethiopia gains in both (Singh +25 % at Debre Zeit with CO2; our Ethiopia chickpea literature change +2.0 %, with F4 falling from a wetter future).
cannot_establish: Mechanisms differ (CO2 in Singh, rainfall in ours) and one site only; abstract only.

reasons: Ethiopia gains in both (Abera mean +10 to +16 % at three sites; our literature change +2.0 %). Both show a wetter-than-hostile future for Ethiopian chickpea, though Abera stresses large year-to-year variability.
cannot_establish: Abera's study period is internally inconsistent (2010-2039 vs 'end of 2040s'); CO2 handling not stated; three sites; cannot compare variability with our period means.

reasons: Qian projects Canadian lentil yield gains (+20 to +28 % in the 2050s), driven by CO2 and warmth with planting-date adaptation. Ours shows a small loss (literature -4.3 %, empirical -1.8 %) with F4 rising from water deficit. Likely reasons: CO2 fertilisation and adaptation, which we exclude, and Qian's process model with soil water vs our P/ETc screening proxy.
cannot_establish: Abstract only; cannot tell whether Qian's climate-only (no-CO2) run would also be negative; 5-GCM CMIP6 ensemble vs one GCM.

reasons: Both show lentil losses in India (Chandran -12 to -31 % with CO2; ours literature -2.0 %, empirical -0.6 %). The mechanism differs: Chandran attributes the loss to warming shortening the reproductive phase, while our small India lentil F4 rise is mostly water deficit.
cannot_establish: Abstract only; one West Bengal site (likely irrigated) vs national rainfed aggregate; mid- and end-century pooled.

reasons: Same as F26 (same model chain): India lentil loss in both, but Chandran's mechanism is heat shortening the reproductive phase while ours is mainly water deficit.
cannot_establish: Not independent of F26; irrigated single site; cannot test magnitudes.

reasons: Tanzania beans: Rippke finds beans the most climate-exposed SSA staple, with transformation needed on ~10 % of Tanzanian bean area by the 2050s. Our Tanzania bean yield change is strongly negative (-17.7 %) and F4 rises with equal heat and water contributions.
cannot_establish: Suitability threshold crossing vs yield change; RCP8.5 median vs SSP2-4.5 one GCM; cannot compare magnitudes.

reasons: Direction and mechanism both agree. Hummel finds most SE African bean area unsuitable by 2050, from heat in NW Tanzania and rainfall decline in E Tanzania. Ours shows a large Tanzanian bean loss with F4 rising equally from heat and water. Hummel's inputs (WorldClim monthly climatology + downscaled GCMs, 2040-2069) are the closest to ours.
cannot_establish: Suitability vs yield; multi-GCM RCP6.0 vs one GCM SSP2-4.5; the drought-induced iron decline is a nutrient-quality pathway our index does not model.

reasons: More frequent drought stress for Brazilian rainfed beans (Heinemann, 2030) matches the rising water component in our Brazil bean F4. Our loss, however, is mainly heat-driven (heat ~0.81 of the F4 change), a mechanism the abstract does not address.
cannot_establish: Abstract only; drought-profile frequency is not yield; 2030 horizon; one state (Goias).

reasons: Antolin projects Brazilian bean yield gains (+5.6 to +9.1 %) mainly from CO2-enhanced photosynthesis; ours projects a large loss (-25.7 %) driven by heat. The difference follows from CO2 inclusion. The paper still finds temperature raises respiration and production risk, which agrees with heat being the negative driver.
cannot_establish: Abstract only; period not stated; cannot obtain a no-CO2 result from the abstract to test whether temperature alone gives a loss.

reasons: Mechanism agrees: Kadiyala's gains come from more rainfall (plus CO2) and its losses from strong warming hastening maturity. Ours: India groundnut change is positive (+1.5 % literature, +6.5 % empirical), with F4 falling because a wetter future outweighs a rising heat part. That resembles the paper's wetter (HadGEM2-ES) case, but the paper's other GCM gives large losses in the Ganges and Indus basins.
cannot_establish: Two-GCM spread shows the sign depends on the GCM, which our single GCM cannot sample; CO2 included; basin results vs national.

reasons: Chandran's West Bengal summer groundnut mostly loses (-33 to +8 % with CO2), while our India groundnut change is a small gain from a wetter kharif.
cannot_establish: Different season (irrigated summer crop vs our rainfed kharif aggregate); one site; abstract only.

reasons: Chandran's full text gives groundnut losses of 3-48 % at the West Bengal site; our India groundnut change is a small gain.
cannot_establish: Same model chain as F33; irrigated summer groundnut at one site cannot represent national rainfed groundnut.

reasons: Rippke finds limited transformation pressure for groundnut in SSA (<15 % of area). Our Nigeria groundnut change is a small gain (+1.5 %), with F4 falling from a wetter future.
cannot_establish: SSA-wide suitability, not Nigeria-specific in the text read; end-century; suitability vs yield.

reasons: With CO2 fixed, Qian's canola production falls at +2.0 C (-0.8 to -5.7 %), matching the sign of our Canada rapeseed loss (-3.2 %, F4 rising from both heat and water). Qian's headline with CO2 and adaptive planting dates is gains, which our index cannot show.
cannot_establish: Warming levels vs 2041-2060; three process models; our rapeseed heat slope is a proxy borrowed from Deryng spring wheat, so heat magnitudes are weakly constrained.

reasons: Both find mustard losses in India from warming (Naresh Kumar about -7.9 % by 2050 without adaptation, worst where seasonal temperatures exceed 25/10 C). Our India rapeseed change is negative (-2.2 %) and the F4 rise is mostly heat.
cannot_establish: Abstract only; SRES-era models; our rapeseed threshold is converted with an assumed diurnal range and the slope is borrowed, so magnitudes and threshold locations are not validated.

reasons: Same direction and mechanism: Boomiraj finds mustard losses driven by maximum-temperature rise; ours is negative and heat-driven for India.
cannot_establish: Abstract only and 2080 horizon only; scenario/GCM not given in abstract; cannot check its regional (east > central > north) pattern.

reasons: Pullens gives agroclimatic risk types (frost in current areas, drought in southern Europe, northern Europe more favourable) for 2081-2100, not yield. Our France rapeseed change is a small loss (-0.4 %) from water deficit; the frost pathway is outside our index.
cannot_establish: Risk indices, end-century, pan-European; France not separated in the abstract; cannot test frost risk at all.

reasons: Six rows from six studies: three global multi-model or multi-method studies (Zhao 2017, Jagermeyr 2021, Deryng 2014), one global sensitivity study (Asseng 2015, abstract), and two India studies (Naresh Kumar 2014 nationwide, abstract; Chandran 2023 one site, full). Without CO2 the evidence agrees on losses, with India among the more sensitive countries. With CO2 (Jagermeyr, Deryng), global and high-latitude wheat gains.
cannot_establish: No verified wheat-specific future study for Russia, Egypt or Brazil beyond the global studies; no study at 2041-2060 SSP2-4.5 with a single CMIP6 GCM; no India study with CMIP6.

reasons: Four rows: Zhao 2017 (India large per-C loss; China/Bangladesh small), Jagermeyr 2021 (global ~0, gains in South Asia with CO2), Soora 2013 (India irrigated -7 % by 2050, rainfed marginal; abstract), Chandran 2023 (one West Bengal site; spans zero without CO2, gains with CO2). Evidence on rice is genuinely mixed; the India irrigated-rice heat loss is the main signal our monthly index does not capture.
cannot_establish: No verified future study for Nigeria, Italy, USA or Brazil rice specifically; no Bangladesh-specific projection read; no CMIP6 India rice study verified.

reasons: Six rows: Zhao 2017, Jagermeyr 2021, Deryng 2014 (shared thresholds), Tigchelaar 2018 (closest method; USA/China/Brazil/Ukraine/India), Ramirez-Cabral 2017 (suitability), Zilli 2020 (Brazil production). The literature agrees on losses in the USA and Brazil and on maize being the most heat-sensitive cereal. Our China/India literature-route gains, which come from wetter conditions, are the main disagreement.
cannot_establish: No verified South Africa-specific future maize study (only Africa-wide statements); no Ukraine study beyond Tigchelaar's export analysis; no India-specific process-model study verified.

reasons: Five rows: Zhao 2017 (weak, non-significant global signal; USA largest loss), Jagermeyr 2021 (USA/Brazil losses, China/high-latitude gains with CO2), Deryng 2014 (shared thresholds), Zilli 2020 (Brazil production losses), Walikar 2018 (Madhya Pradesh, small 2050 declines, GCM not stated). The direction is mixed and depends strongly on CO2 treatment.
cannot_establish: No verified future study for Argentina, Russia or South Africa specifically; the Brazil CROPGRO study by Moura da Silva et al. 2021 (EJA) could not be read (abstract not accessible); no CMIP6 India soybean study verified.

reasons: Three rows from two studies: Singh et al. 2014 (India and Ethiopia sites, CO2-inclusive, abstract only) and Abera et al. 2026 (central Ethiopia, CORDEX RCP4.5, full text). Ethiopia gains in both and in ours; India is site-dependent (north/central gains with CO2, south loses).
cannot_establish: No verified future projection for Australia, Turkiye, Russia, USA or China chickpea; no India study separating climate from CO2 was readable; Singh 2014 full text not accessible (ICRISAT repository unreachable).

reasons: Three rows from two research groups: Qian et al. 2026 (Canadian Prairies, CMIP6, gains with CO2 and planting adaptation; abstract only) and Chandran et al. 2022/2023 (one West Bengal site, India, losses of 12-31 %; abstract and full text of the companion paper). The evidence splits by region and CO2 treatment.
cannot_establish: No verified future lentil study for Australia, USA, Russia, China or Ethiopia; the India evidence is a single irrigated site from one group; the Canadian study's no-CO2 result is not in the abstract.

reasons: Four rows: Rippke 2016 and Hummel 2018 (SSA/SE Africa incl. Tanzania; beans the most exposed staple; heat and rainfall mechanisms; Hummel adds a drought-driven iron decline), Heinemann 2017 (Brazil, Goias: more frequent drought by 2030; abstract) and Antolin 2021 (Brazil yield gains driven by CO2; abstract). Tanzania evidence agrees with our loss; Brazil evidence conflicts on direction because of CO2.
cannot_establish: No verified future common-bean study for India, Myanmar, China, USA or Belarus (FAOSTAT 'Beans, dry' covers several Phaseolus/Vigna species in Asia, which none of these studies addresses); Beebe/Ramirez-Villegas global bean heat projections not verified.

reasons: Four rows: Kadiyala 2021 (India, two GCMs, sign depends on the GCM; rain gains vs heat losses; full text), Chandran 2022/2023 (West Bengal irrigated summer groundnut, losses), Rippke 2016 (SSA incl. Nigeria, limited transformation pressure). India evidence is mixed and GCM-dependent, and our wetter-future gain sits within Kadiyala's range.
cannot_establish: No verified future groundnut study for China, USA or Brazil; Singh et al. 2014 (MASGC, India and West Africa) abstract reports only trait-adaptation gains, not baseline impacts, and its full text (ICRISAT) was unreachable; Nigeria-specific projections not found.

reasons: Four rows: Qian 2019 (Canada canola: gains with CO2, losses with CO2 fixed), Naresh Kumar 2016 and Boomiraj 2010 (India mustard losses from warming; abstracts), Pullens 2019 (Europe winter rapeseed risk types, end-century; abstract). Evidence agrees that warming alone lowers yields in India and Canada.
